newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives deny rift over food scare.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives deny rift over food scare.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives, hit by yet another controversy over food safety, on Friday denied reports of a cabinet rift over a study on abattoir hygiene conditions.

But bad news abounded for the government in the run-up to a general election that has to be called by May. Latest opinion polls showed the Conservatives trailing the opposition Labour Party by up to 26 points with time running out fast.
Prime Minister John Major, his leadership constantly battered by party mutinies over Britain's role in Europe, has sought to present a united pre-election front.

But headlines proliferated on Friday about cabinet conflict on a report which pinpointed unhygienic conditions in abattoirs that could have spread disease to meat supplies. In Scotland, 20 people have been killed by an E.coli food poisoning outbreak.
Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth launched into a damaging limitation exercise after reports that he was "incandescent" with rage over Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg's handling of the report.
Forsyth, whose office took the unusual step on Thursday night of issuing a statement to say it had never seen the food poisoning report, insisted there was no cabinet split.

"What I am angry about is the suggestion that there is a rift between Douglas Hogg and me on handling the issue and I am angry about the suggestion that ministers knew about this report and somewhow sought to suppress it," he told BBC Radio.
But Labour was scornful, with their Scottish spokesman George Robertson claiming: "The people who are supposed to be running the country don't know what is going on."
Hogg, already under fire over his handling of the mad cow crisis, denied in parliament he had suppressed the report.

Professor Hugh Pennington, the scientist appointed by the government to look into the E.coli outbreak, said he had not been told about the report and that it could have helped him in his investigation.

Labour said it believed the government may have held the report back because it would have come on top of a ministerial admission of a possible link between mad cow disease, or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), and its human equivalent Creutzfeld-Jakob Disease (CJD).

The crisis over mad cow disease resulted in a European Union worldwide ban on British beef exports. The ban has crippled the country's beef industry and led to two widespread culling operations which have cost the government 3.5 billion pounds ($5.7 billion).
